RepoMark: A Code Usage Auditing Framework for Code Large Language Models

Wenjie Qu1, Yuguang Zhou1, Bo Wang1, Wengrui Zheng1, Yuexin Li1, Jinyuan Jia2, Jiaheng Zhang1 Affiliation: 1 National University of Singapore, 2 Penn State University
Abstract

The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code generation has transformed software development by automating coding tasks with unprecedented efficiency. However, the training of these models on open-source code repositories (e.g., from GitHub) raises critical ethical and legal concerns, particularly regarding data authorization and open-source license compliance. Developers are increasingly questioning whether model trainers have obtained proper authorization before using repositories for training, especially given the lack of transparency in data collection.

To address these concerns, we propose a novel data marking framework RepoMark to audit the data usage of code LLMs. Our method enables repository owners to verify whether their code has been used in training, while ensuring semantic preservation, imperceptibility, and theoretical false detection rate (FDR) guarantees. By generating multiple semantically equivalent code variants, RepoMark introduces data marks into the code files, and during detection, RepoMark leverages a novel ranking-based hypothesis test to detect memorization within the model. Compared to prior data auditing approaches, RepoMark significantly enhances sample efficiency, allowing effective auditing even when the user’s repository possesses only a small number of code files.

Experiments demonstrate that RepoMark achieves a detection success rate over 90% on small code repositories under a strict FDR guarantee of 5%. This represents a significant advancement over existing data marking techniques, all of which only achieve accuracy below 55% under identical settings. This further validates RepoMark as a robust, theoretically sound, and promising solution for enhancing transparency in code LLM training, which can safeguard the rights of repository owners.

I Introduction

The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) in code generation has revolutionized software development, enabling developers to automate coding tasks with unprecedented efficiency. Open-source communities such as GitHub, which maintain a large set of code repositories, have become the main source of training data for code LLMs [1, 2, 3]. However, the use of publicly available code repositories to train these models has raised critical ethical and legal questions.

A primary concern is data authorization—specifically, whether model developers have obtained proper consent from code authors to use their repositories for training purposes. While source code itself may not always constitute personal data, developers’ rights regarding the usage and distribution of their code align with broader data protection principles established by regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [4] in Europe, which grant data owners the right to know how their data is used. Nevertheless, the training of machine learning models often suffers from a pervasive lack of transparency. Model trainers rarely disclose the details of the origin of their training data [5], and the opaque data collection processes employed in training code LLMs make it difficult to audit whether proper authorization was obtained from repository owners for model training. This lack of transparency is especially concerning given the emergence of commercial products such as GitHub Copilot [6], Amazon CodeWhisperer [1], Cursor [3], Tabnine [7], and Codeium [8]. Exploiting source code without authorization to train models for commercial purposes directly violates the rights and contributions of original authors and undermines the spirit of the open-source community.

Given these ethical and legal concerns, tracing the data usage of code LLMs has become a pressing issue. The most prevalent approach to address this challenge is data auditing [5], which enables data owners to verify whether their data has been used to train a machine learning (ML) model. Existing data auditing methods can be categorized into passive data auditing and proactive data auditing. Passive data auditing, commonly called membership inference [9], infers if a data sample is a member of an ML model’s training set without modifying the training data. In contrast, proactive data auditing, a.k.a. data marking [10], embeds marks such as word perturbations into data prior to publication, enabling detection methods to exploit statistical signals introduced during marking to detect unauthorized data usage. In general, proactive data auditing is more powerful than passive data auditing and often achieves higher detection accuracy [5]. Therefore, we focus on the proactive data auditing paradigm for detecting unauthorized data usage for code LLMs.

To effectively audit the data usage of code LLMs, the data marking method should satisfy four properties: (1) Preservation of Semantics: The modifications introduced by the marking method must retain the original code’s semantics. (2) Imperceptibility: The code marks should be difficult for model trainers to identify, as they are incentivized to remove the marked code files to avoid being caught. (3) Sample-Efficiency: In the real world, individuals often have very few repositories, and their projects may be quite small-scale with only 10–50 code files. The method should retain sufficient accuracy in detecting model training on such small-scale repositories. (4) FDR Guarantee: The method should have a guarantee on false detection rate (FDR). FDR is defined as the probability of incorrectly flagging a target model as having been trained on a user’s repository when no such training occurred. A theoretical FDR guarantee is imperative, as false accusations against the model trainer could lead to significant reputational harm and ethical breaches.

However, existing data marking schemes fail to satisfy the four aforementioned properties simultaneously. Firstly, data marking solutions for language models such as Wei et al. [11] and Huang et al. [5] (CCS’24) cannot be straightforwardly adapted to the code domain. For instance, Huang et al.[5] relies on paraphrasing for data mark injection, a strategy that is infeasible for code. Wei et al. [11] append long random sequences to the data as marks, which can be easily detected and removed by the model trainers. Secondly, for data marking methods designed for code, CodeMark [12] (FSE’23) lacks sample efficiency, requiring the data owner to control a considerable proportion of the training dataset (e.g., 40%), which renders it ineffective for auditing individual repositories that typically occupy only a tiny fraction of the overall training corpus. Furthermore, most data auditing methods cannot provide a rigorous guarantee on FDR [5]. Although methods like Radioactive Data [13] and Huang et al. [5] can provide a guarantee on FDR, they remain inapplicable to code data.

To simultaneously achieve the four properties, we first propose a novel data marking framework on general data modalities, offering enhanced sample efficiency and a provable FDR guarantee, addressing the last two properties. Based on our general data marking framework, we further introduce RepoMark , a data auditing framework with concrete marking and detection algorithms tailored to the code domain, thereby fulfilling all four desired properties.

General data marking framework. In the marking phase of our general data marking framework, the data owner generates mm similar variants of each data sample (i.e., a file in the code repository). Then a randomly chosen version is published while the other versions are kept private. Later, during the detection phase, for each data sample, we compute the rank of the published version among all generated versions based on the loss when substituting them into the code. We then perform a hypothesis test on the sum of these ranks across all data samples to assess whether the model has been trained on the data owner’s data.

The core idea of our framework is to aggregate the memorization signal represented as ranks of each data sample to perform detection. Due to the randomness in the selection of the published version, if the model is not trained on a data sample, the rank of the published sample will be uniformly distributed among {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\}. In contrast, if the model is trained on a data sample, then the rank is likely to be biased towards 11. Our detection algorithm leverages the summation of the ranks across different data samples to amplify this bias for detection. Due to the uniform property of the rank distribution under the untrained case, the FDR of our method is theoretically upper-bounded.

Adaptation to code domain. The remaining challenge is how to design a dedicated marking algorithm and its corresponding detection algorithm for code that fits into our framework. The critical property our marking method has to satisfy is that, the mm variants of code it generates all preserve the program semantics, while the difference between the mm variants and the original code should be imperceptible to the model trainer.

To preserve the program semantics of marked code, our marking algorithm focuses on renaming local variables. For each code file, we select one variable to rename. A similar variable set of size mm is generated based on token likelihoods computed by an oracle code LLM. The selected variable is then renamed to a variable randomly chosen from this set. The different mm variable names chosen from this set correspond to the mm versions of the code file required by our general marking framework. The integration of code variable renaming into our general data marking framework yields RepoMark, which satisfies all four desired properties.

We further improve the sample efficiency of RepoMark by injecting multiple marks for long code files. When the model is not trained on the marked file, the randomness in publication selection ensures that, during detection, the ranks of different injected marks within the same file are independent of each other and uniformly distributed over {1,…,m}\{1,\dots,m\}. This property guarantees the correctness of the detection of multiple marks per file and greatly improves the sample efficiency of our framework.

Experimental results show that RepoMark consistently achieves high accuracy across different code LLMs and datasets. When auditing training data usage of the CodeParrot model [14], RepoMark can identify more than 90% of the repositories used for training, under a 5% FDR guarantee. Under the same FDR, the best data marking baseline can only correctly detect about 54% of the repositories. Additionally, the experiments show that RepoMark achieves strong imperceptibility: the marked code has an average perplexity of 1.11, closely matching the unmarked code’s perplexity of 1.04.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose a general data auditing framework with a theoretical FDR guarantee and better sample-efficiency.

  • •

    Building on our proposed paradigm, we introduce RepoMark, a novel data auditing framework for code LLMs that achieves significantly higher sample efficiency and provides a theoretical guarantee on the FDR.

  • •

    We validate the effectiveness of RepoMark through extensive experiments. Experiments show that it achieves high accuracy in detecting the training data usage of code LLMs and significantly outperforms all previous baselines. For reproducibility, we anonymously provide our source code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/repomark-7E4B.

II Background and related work

II-A Code large language models

Large language models. Modern large language models (LLMs) typically utilize the Transformer architecture [15]. The LLM’s input context consists of a sequence of tokens, denoted as ⟨s1,s2,⋯,sL⟩\left\langle s_{1},s_{2},\cdots,s_{L}\right\rangle. These LLMs predict subsequent tokens in an autoregressive manner. We denote the vocabulary of an LLM as 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The LLM predicts the next token sL+1s_{L+1} by first mapping the token sequence into a logit vector z∈ℝ|𝒱|z\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}:

z=𝖫𝖫𝖬⁡(⟨s1,s2,⋯,sL⟩)z=\mathsf{LLM}(\left\langle s_{1},s_{2},\cdots,s_{L}\right\rangle)

Then the model uses a decoding strategy to decide the next token sL+1s_{L+1} based on the logit vector. Commonly adopted strategies include top-kk sampling [16], which restricts the next token choice to the kk most probable tokens based on logits, and nucleus sampling [17], which samples from the smallest possible set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold pp. The newly generated token sL+1s_{L+1} is then appended to the model input context to generate the next token. This autoregressive process repeats until a stop condition is met, typically when a special end-of-sequence token is generated or when a maximum sequence length is reached.

Code large language models. Code LLMs are a specialized class of large language models designed to assist developers with coding tasks in software development. Many code LLMs are obtained by fine-tuning general-purpose language models on code datasets, such as CodeParrot [14] and StarCoder [18]. However, some prominent code LLMs, such as InCoder [19], are trained from scratch solely on code data.

II-B Membership inference attack

Membership inference attack (MIA) is a type of confidentiality attack in machine learning, which aims to infer whether a particular data sample has been used to train a target ML model [9, 20, 21, 22]. Existing MIA methods can be classified into loss-based attacks [20, 21, 23, 24] and shadow model-based attacks [9, 22]. Loss-based MIAs are based on the simple observation [21] that training a model minimizes the loss on the training set, which leads to the loss of the training samples lower than that of samples outside the training set. Shadow model-based attacks leverage trained shadow models to mimic the target model. This line of work incur higher computational cost compared to loss-based MIAs. MIA have been explored for various types of ML models, including image classifiers [9, 20, 22], diffusion models [25, 26, 27], and language models [28, 29, 30].

MIA can serve as a passive data auditing method, as it does not require any prior modification or marking of the training data. Most existing MIAs operate at the instance level, aiming to identify whether a single example was part of the training data. A few works [31, 32, 33] have generalized MIA to the dataset level, detecting whether a given dataset was used to train a model by aggregating instance-level MIA results across data points. This line of work is more closely related to our scenario, where a repository owner seeks to detect whether a code LLM has been trained on their code repository. However, applying MIA to audit the data usage of code LLMs faces a critical limitation: although thresholds for MIA methods can be calibrated under experimental conditions by setting an empirical FDR using known member and non-member labels, in real-world auditing scenarios, where such labels are unavailable, there is no guarantee on the FDR of MIA methods.

II-C Data marking

Data marking is a type of proactive technique that allows a data owner to audit the use of their data in a target ML model [5, 34, 35, 36, 13, 11]. Such methods usually consist of a marking algorithm that embeds marks into data and a detection algorithm that tests whether the data has been used to train a given model.

II-C1 Data marking for image classifiers

Radioactive Data [13] is a classical data marking method for image classifier auditing. In the marking phase,  [13] embeds randomly sampled marks into a subset of the training dataset. In the detection phase, it detects whether the parameters of the final layer of the target image classifier are correlated with the selected marks. The drawback of  [13] is that this method requires the data owner to have white-box access to the model parameters, which is not realistic in real-world data auditing.

Another line of work on data auditing for image classifiers [34, 35, 36] is based on backdoor attacks [37]. In these approaches, the data owner injects marks using the same way as a backdoor attack, and data usage is detected by observing predictable misclassifications of backdoored images. However, as pointed out by Huang et al. [5], these methods lack rigorous guarantees on their FDR.

Nonetheless, the significant modality gap between image and code makes it difficult to adapt these methods to the code domain.

II-C2 Data marking for LLMs

Wei et al. [11] is the first data marking method for LLMs. At the marking phase, the data owner generates a random character sequence and appends it to each of his data samples to publish. During the detection phase, the data owner generates multiple random sequences and appends them to the raw data he holds, and measures the memorization of each random sequence. They empirically construct the distribution of memorized token length under the null hypothesis by measuring the memorization of different random sequences. Then they leverage hypothesis testing to check whether the memorized token length of the actual published data is much higher than the mean of the memorized token length under null hypothesis, thereby determining whether the data is trained by the LLM. A significant limitation of this method when applied to code LLMs is that appending random sequences as code comments to code files can be easily detected and automatically removed by the model trainer.

A recent data marking framework by Huang et al. [5] supports both image classifiers and language models. To the best of our knowledge, it is the only work that provides an FDR guarantee for data usage auditing under black-box access to the model. Prior to data publication, the data owner generates two slightly modified versions of each raw data sample, publishes one version chosen uniformly at random, and keeps the other private. During the detection phase, the data owner computes the loss for both the published and private versions. The number of published samples whose loss is smaller than that of their private counterparts serves as a score for measuring data infringement. The key insight is that if the published data are not used to train the model, the probability that a published version has a smaller loss than its private version is 12\frac{1}{2}, due to the randomness in choosing the public version. By performing a hypothesis test on this score, the detection algorithm can provide a provable guarantee on the FDR. However, [5] is not directly applicable to the code domain. In addition, its detection accuracy degrades significantly for repositories with few files, limiting its practical utility.

II-C3 Data marking for code LLMs

To the best of our knowledge, CodeMark [12] is the only work focusing on building a data marking method for code LLMs. It embeds imperceptible marks into code while maintaining functionality based on semantic-preserving transformations (SPTs). Its detection relies on statistically verifying co-appearance patterns of transformed code pairs in model outputs. This type of signal is relatively weak. Therefore, the method requires modifying a significant proportion of the entire dataset to ensure accurate detection. However, this approach is impractical for auditing code repositories that contain only a dozen files. With limited content, it is difficult to embed sufficient signals, leading to low detection accuracy.

III Problem formulation

III-A Threat model

In our paper, we consider two parties: the code repository owner and the trainer of the code LLM. The repository owner holds a set {x1,x2,…,xN}\left\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{N}\right\} of code files that will be uploaded to a code platform like GitHub. The model trainer aims to train a code model 𝖫𝖫𝖬\mathsf{LLM} with strong coding capability on a large set of code data.

The model trainer assembles a training dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} by collecting the code online from many repositories without authorization. As such, after publication, the repository owner’s data constitutes a subset of the model trainer’s collected dataset (i.e., some portion of {x1,x2,…,xN}\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{N}\} is contained in 𝒟\mathcal{D}). The code LLM trainer trains a model on the collected data using a learning algorithm. Then the model trainer deploys the trained code LLM to provide service to consumers (e.g., to monetize the trained code LLM).

The repository owner aims to detect whether the code LLM trainer has used their data. To achieve this, the owner must apply an auditing method that can identify data misuse if the trainer has incorporated the published code, relying solely on black-box access to the deployed model. In other words, the repository owner has no knowledge of the code LLM’s architecture or parameters. Following the threat model adopted in prior data marking works [5, 11, 13], in most parts of the paper, we assume that the data owner has access to the output logits of the code LLM during inference. Additionally, in Section IV-E, we extend our algorithm to support a more restrictive logits access setting aligned with the OpenAI API [38].

III-B Design goals

As mentioned in Section I, an effective code LLM data usage auditing method should achieve following properties:

  • •

    Preservation of semantics: All modifications should preserve the original program’s semantics.

  • •

    Imperceptibility: The modifications to the code should be difficult for the trainer of the code LLM to detect.

  • •

    Sample-Efficient: The method should accurately detect training data usage even when the number of code files nn is small (e.g., 10–50 files).

  • •

    FDR Guarantee: The method should provide a statistical upper bound on its FDR, which is the probability of incorrectly identifying the code LLM as having been trained on the target repository when it was not.

An FDR guarantee of pp limits the probability of wrongly accusing a model of training on a protected repository to below pp, which is critical for preventing false claims and associated ethical risks. Under a given FDR constraint, the effectiveness of auditing is measured by the detection success rate (DSR), defined as # of correctly identified trained repositories# of repositories actually trained on\frac{\text{\# of correctly identified trained repositories}}{\text{\# of repositories actually trained on}}. A high DSR means the method can detect most training repositories, which is important for auditing.

Although probabilistic evidence is not as definitive as deterministic proof, it is often sufficient and widely accepted in legal practice. A classic example is DNA matching: it does not claim that ”this DNA definitely belongs to the suspect,” but rather that ”the suspect’s DNA matches, and the probability of a random individual also matching is 1 in 10,000.” Moreover, in copyright infringement cases, evidence only needs to meet the lower ”preponderance of the evidence” standard [39] under US civil law, requiring just >50%>50\% likelihood of validity. All these examples demonstrate the practical potential of data auditing methods that offer strong FDR guarantees when providing deterministic results is not feasible.

IV Methodology

IV-A New Data auditing framework

We first present a novel sample-efficient framework with FDR guarantee used to detect if an ML model has been trained on the data owner’s data {x1,⋯,xN}\{x_{1},\cdots,x_{N}\}. This general-purpose framework can potentially support a wide range of data modalities and serves as the foundation of RepoMark. The core idea is to generate multiple semantically equivalent versions for each data sample, randomly select one version to publish, and use the sum of the loss ranks of the published versions to perform hypothesis testing for detection.

At the marking phase, the data owner creates mm different equivalent versions of each xix_{i}, i∈{1,⋯,N}i\in\{1,\cdots,N\}, denoted as xi1,xi2,⋯,ximx_{i}^{1},x_{i}^{2},\cdots,x_{i}^{m}. For each i∈{1,⋯,N}i\in\{1,\cdots,N\}, the data owner uniformly randomly chooses an index vi←${1,2,⋯,N}v_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\$}}{{\leftarrow}}\{1,2,\cdots,N\}; and publishes xivix_{i}^{v_{i}} while keeping all of the other versions of xix_{i} private. During the detection phase, for each data sample xix_{i}, we query the target model with all mm of its versions and compute the corresponding losses, forming the set {ℓ⁡(xi1),…,ℓ⁡(xim)}\{\ell(x_{i}^{1}),\ldots,\ell(x_{i}^{m})\}. Our detection algorithm merely relies on the rank of ℓ⁡(xivi)\ell(x_{i}^{v_{i}}) in the loss of mm variants, namely, 𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)}CLOSE\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x_{i}^{1}),\cdots,\ell(x_{i}^{m})\},OPENℓ⁡(xivi))\ell(x_{i}^{v_{i}})). Using ranks enables rigorous probabilistic guarantee analysis, which is difficult to achieve by analyzing loss values directly, as the latter requires assumptions about the distribution of the loss values across the mm variants.

Our key theoretical insight is that if the model is not trained on xivix_{i}^{v_{i}}, define 𝗋𝗄⁡(U,u)\mathsf{rk}(U,u) computes the rank of uu among the set UU in ascending order, we have 𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)},ℓ⁡(xivi))∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆⁡({1,2,⋯,m})\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x_{i}^{1}),\cdots,\ell(x_{i}^{m})\},\ell(x_{i}^{v_{i}}))\sim\mathsf{Uniform}(\{1,2,\cdots,m\}). The uniform randomness stems from the random sampling of viv_{i}, which removes the potential bias in different versions of xix_{i}. However, if the model is trained on xivix_{i}^{v_{i}}, since the model is not trained on the other versions, ℓ⁡(xivi)\ell(x_{i}^{v_{i}}) is more likely to have a small rank in 1,2,⋯,m1,2,\cdots,m (e.g., less than m2\frac{m}{2}).

Now, we can leverage hypothesis testing to build a detection algorithm with a rigorous FDR guarantee. The statistical quantity SS we consider for hypothesis testing is the sum of the ranks of all published data, formally defined as S=∑i=1N𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)},ℓ⁡(xivi))S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x^{1}_{i}),\cdots,\ell(x^{m}_{i})\},\ell(x^{v_{i}}_{i})).

We set the rank sum threshold as TT. If the model is not trained on the target dataset {x1,⋯,xN}\{x_{1},\cdots,x_{N}\}, then each 𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)}CLOSE\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x^{1}_{i}),\cdots,\ell(x^{m}_{i})\} ,ℓ(xivi)),\ell(x^{v_{i}}_{i})) is uniformly distributed among {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\}. By the central limit theorem, SS will be close to its expectation N⁡(m+1)2\frac{N(m+1)}{2} with high probability. Thus, for thresholds TT less than N⁡(m+1)2\frac{N(m+1)}{2} with sufficient margin, the event S>TS>T occurs with high probability if the model is not trained on the dataset x1,⋯,xN{x_{1},\cdots,x_{N}}. In contrast, if the model is trained on the target dataset {x1,⋯,xN}\{x_{1},\cdots,x_{N}\}, for each sample xix_{i}, 𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)},ℓ⁡(xivi))\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x^{1}_{i}),\cdots,\ell(x^{m}_{i})\},\ell(x^{v_{i}}_{i})) is likely to be smaller than m2\frac{m}{2}, and SS would be much more likely smaller than TT. As such, the detection problem of our scheme can be formulated to test the following hypothesis:

  • •

    H0:𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)},ℓ⁡(xivi))∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆⁡({1,2,⋯,m})H_{0}:\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x^{1}_{i}),\cdots,\ell(x^{m}_{i})\},\ell(x^{v_{i}}_{i}))\sim\mathsf{Uniform}(\{1,2,\cdots,m\})

Under H0H_{0}, SS follows the distribution of the sum of NN i.i.d variables, each uniformly distributed among {1,2,…,m}\{1,2,…,m\}. As such, the data owner can reject H0H_{0} or accept H0H_{0} according to the value of SS. The FDR of this testing procedure is provably upper-bounded, as the bound corresponds to the probability of rejecting H0H_{0} when it is actually true. Given the upper-bounded FDR, rejecting H0H_{0} implies that, with high probability, the target model has been trained on the published samples. The FDR guarantee could be adjusted by altering TT.

IV-B Semantic preservation and imperceptible code marking

Building on our previously introduced data marking framework, we design a concrete marking algorithm specifically tailored for code data. This algorithm allows the data owner to generate multiple semantically equivalent variants of the original code while preserving functionality and readability. Importantly, it satisfies all the desired properties outlined in Section III-B. In this section, we focus on the core setting of embedding a single mark into each code file. We further extend this method to support embedding multiple marks within a single file in Section IV-D, which significantly increases sample-efficiency in our method.

The preservation of code semantics is a critical property our code marking scheme has to achieve, because disruptions to code semantics would negatively impact the repository’s readability and functionality, hindering our scheme’s real-world deployment. Imperceptibility is also important for a practical marking algorithm, as the malicious model trainers are always incentivized to remove the marks to avoid tracing.

To achieve both code semantics preservation and imperceptibility simultaneously, we come up with a natural strategy of only renaming variables. In our marking algorithm, we only rename variables that are local variable and only consist of a single token. To apply a mark to a code file, we first need to select a variable to rename. Once a variable is selected, we use an oracle model (another code LLM) to propose alternative variable names, forming a similar variable name set of size mm. Each of the mm versions of the code file is generated by renaming the selected variable with one of these mm alternatives.

A natural strawman approach is to randomly select some variables and construct the alternative list using their synonyms. However, this approach is limited by the typically small number of synonyms available for each variable. Since higher values of mm lead to better detection accuracy, we instead focus on variables that admit a large set of alternative names. Crucially, these alternatives must have similar predicted likelihoods under the oracle model. This requires the original variable name to have a relatively low predicted likelihood, so that more alternative names fall within a similar likelihood range.

This leads to a key insight: we should prefer variables whose names have a low likelihood when predicted by the oracle model. However, a challenge arises because variables typically appear multiple times within a file, and their predicted likelihood varies across occurrences. To address this, we determine a variable’s likelihood based on its first occurrence. This choice is motivated by an important observation: code LLMs find it significantly harder to predict a variable’s name at its first appearance compared to later ones. This is intuitive—once a variable has been introduced, subsequent references are easier to guess, both for models and humans. Predicting the first appearance is much harder as it demands reasoning from local code patterns, function names, and broader coding conventions, rather than relying on repetition.

In conclusion, we focus on single-token variables whose first occurrence has a relatively high logits rank under the oracle model. Let PP denote the logits rank of the token corresponding to the variable name. We require that P≥RP\geq R, where RR is a predefined threshold, and we ensure R≫mR\gg m to allow enough similar candidates. For each selected variable, we form its similar variable name set TT by collecting tokens whose logits ranks fall in the range [P−m2,P+m2)[P-\frac{m}{2},P+\frac{m}{2}). Finally, to guarantee that renaming does not alter program semantics, we parse the code file using a lightweight static analysis tool to build its abstract syntax tree (AST). For each token in set TT, we rename all occurrences of the target variable in the AST to produce each marked version of the code file.

Intuitively, our marking method can be viewed as a heuristic that renames variables whose original names ”surprise” the oracle code LLM, replacing them with alternative names that have similar oracle rankings. The reason why we choose these ”surprising” variables is that, if we choose variables that have small oracle ranks, to achieve imperceptibility, we can only choose other tokens that also have small rankings, resulting in a small search space of equivalent variants (i.e., small mm). Choosing to rename these ”surprising” variables allows for a much larger mm, thereby increasing the information contained in the rank and improving detection accuracy.

The imperceptibility property of this strategy can be explained from the perspective of the perplexity of the oracle model. The perplexity depends on the logits of each token. These mm different versions have similar logit ranks measured by the oracle model, and LLM logits typically satisfy a long-tail distribution. Since P≫mP\gg m, the logits of all mm different versions are likely to be in the long tail of the logits distribution, which makes their logits value very similar to each other. This indicates that, the change to the code caused by renaming variables is imperceptible measured by the perplexity of the oracle model.

The complete marking procedure for a single code file is formalized in Algorithm 1. During repository-level auditing, this algorithm is applied iteratively to each file.

IV-C Detection with FDR guarantee

In this section, we provide a detailed description and analysis of RepoMark’s detection algorithm, with an illustration provided in Figure . Its high-level idea is to capture the ranks of the published version in different code files, and test whether their sum deviates significantly from the H0H_{0} case.

We first analyze the rank distribution under H0H_{0}. We denote the code LLM weight as ww, and it follows an unknown distribution WW. Target model with weight ww accepts the token sequence xx as input and predicts the probability of variable name tt being the next token after xx. For simplicity, we denote the corresponding cross-entropy loss as f⁡(w,x,t)f(w,x,t). We denote the mm versions of variable renamings as {t1,⋯,tm}\{t^{1},\cdots,t^{m}\}, and the published version’s ID as r∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆⁡(1,⋯,m)r\sim\mathsf{Uniform}(1,\cdots,m). For the rank of the published version 𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w,x,t1),⋯,f⁡(w,x,tm)},f⁡(w,x,tr))\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w,x,t^{1}),\cdots,f(w,x,t^{m})\},f(w,x,t^{r})), we have the following theorem:

Theorem 1.

Under H0H_{0}, 𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w,x,t1),⋯,f⁡(w,x,tm)}𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w,x,t^{1}),\cdots,f(w,x,t^{m})\} ,f(w,x,tr)),f(w,x,t^{r})) is uniformly distributed among {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\}.

Proof.

Under H0H_{0}, ww is independent with rr. ∀k∈{1,⋯,m}\forall k\in\{1,\cdots,m\}, we have:

Pr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w,x,t1),⋯,f⁡(w,x,tm)},f⁡(w,x,tr))=k)=∑y=1m∑w′∈WPr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w′,x,t1),⋯},f⁡(w′,x,ty))=k)Pr⁡(r=y,w=w′)=∑y=1m∑w′∈WPr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w′,x,t1),⋯},f⁡(w′,x,ty))=k)⋅1m​Pr⁡(w=w′)=1m​∑w′∈WPr⁡(w=w′)∑y=1mPr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w′,x,t1),⋯},f⁡(w′,x,ty))=k)\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w,x,t^{1}),\cdots,f(w,x,t^{m})\},f(w,x,t^{r}))=k)\\ =&\sum_{y=1}^{m}\sum_{w^{\prime}\in W}\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w^{\prime},x,t^{1}),\cdots\},f(w^{\prime},x,t^{y}))=k)\\ &\Pr(r=y,w=w^{\prime})\\ =&\sum_{y=1}^{m}\sum_{w^{\prime}\in W}\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w^{\prime},x,t^{1}),\cdots\},f(w^{\prime},x,t^{y}))=k)\\ &\cdot\frac{1}{m}\Pr(w=w^{\prime})\\ =&\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w^{\prime}\in W}\Pr(w=w^{\prime})\\ &\sum_{y=1}^{m}\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w^{\prime},x,t^{1}),\cdots\},f(w^{\prime},x,t^{y}))=k)\end{aligned} (1)

Given w′,xw^{\prime},x, {f⁡(w′,x,t1),⋯,f⁡(w′,x,tm)}\{f(w^{\prime},x,t^{1}),\cdots,f(w^{\prime},x,t^{m})\} is a deterministic set, with only one element in it having rank kk. Thus, ∀k∈{1,⋯,m}\forall k\in\{1,\cdots,m\}, we have:

∑y=1mPr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w′,x,t1),⋯},f⁡(w′,x,ty))=k)=1\displaystyle\sum_{y=1}^{m}\Pr\left(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w^{\prime},x,t^{1}),\cdots\},f(w^{\prime},x,t^{y}))=k\right)=1

Substituting the above equation into Equation 1, we have:

Pr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w,x,t1),⋯,f⁡(w,x,tm)},f⁡(w,x,tr))=k)\displaystyle\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w,x,t^{1}),\cdots,f(w,x,t^{m})\},f(w,x,t^{r}))=k)
=\displaystyle= 1m​∑w′∈WPr⁡(w=w′)=1m\displaystyle\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w^{\prime}\in W}\Pr(w=w^{\prime})=\frac{1}{m}

∎

The above theorem shows that when ww is not trained on the published version trt^{r}, the rank of the published version’s loss among the losses of all versions {t1,⋯,tm}\{t^{1},\cdots,t^{m}\} is uniformly distributed over {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\}. This uniform randomness essentially stems from the uniform selection of rr from {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\}.

When ww is trained on the published version trt^{r}, ww becomes dependent on rr, and the rank is no longer uniformly distributed over {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\}. While the complex behavior of LLMs makes the exact rank distribution difficult to characterize, training-induced memorization should bias ranks toward smaller values. In particular, the untrained mean rank is m+12\frac{m+1}{2}, whereas the trained mean should be significantly smaller.

There are multiple code files in one repository. Therefore, we can leverage the rank sum to aggregate the message delivered by the mark in each code file. With more injected marks (larger nn), the distribution of the rank sum of the nn marks under the untrained case is more concentrated around n⁡(m+1)2\frac{n(m+1)}{2}, as we can see in Figure 3.

We denote the rank sum of different mark positions as SS and the hyperparameter of rank sum threshold as TT. If the model is not trained on the target repository, by the central limit theorem, SS will be close to its expectation n⁡(m+1)2\frac{n(m+1)}{2} with high probability. Therefore, if the model is not trained on the target repository, for T<n⁡(m+1)2T<\frac{n(m+1)}{2} with a sufficient gap, Pr⁡(S≤T)\Pr(S\leq T) will be very small.In contrast, if the model is trained on the target repository, each 𝗋𝗄⁡(ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim),ℓ⁡(xivi))\mathsf{rk}({\ell(x^{1}_{i}),\cdots,\ell(x^{m}_{i})},\ell(x^{v_{i}}_{i})) is much more likely to have a value smaller than m2\frac{m}{2}, and SS would likely be smaller than TT.

As such, the detection problem of our scheme can be formulated as the following hypothesis test:

  • •

    H0:𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)},ℓ⁡(xivi))∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿𝗈𝗋𝗆⁡({1,2,⋯,m})H_{0}:\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x^{1}_{i}),\cdots,\ell(x^{m}_{i})\},\ell(x^{v_{i}}_{i}))\sim\mathsf{Uniform}(\{1,2,\cdots,m\})

  • •

    H1:𝗋𝗄⁡({ℓ⁡(xi1),⋯,ℓ⁡(xim)},ℓ⁡(xivi))H_{1}:\mathsf{rk}(\{\ell(x_{i}^{1}),\cdots,\ell(x_{i}^{m})\},\ell(x_{i}^{v_{i}})) is biased towards smaller values

Under H0H_{0}, SS follows the distribution of the sum of nn i.i.d random variables uniformly distributed among {1,2,⋯,m}\{1,2,\cdots,m\}. The data owner can reject H0H_{0} or accept H0H_{0} based on whether S>TS>T. In other words, the data owner detects whether their repository is trained by the target code LLM according to whether S≤TS\leq T. The FDR of this test is provably upper-bounded by the Type I error—the probability that H0H_{0} is incorrectly rejected—which corresponds to the probability that the sum of these nn uniform i.i.d random variables is less than or equal to TT. Thus, the FDR guarantee could be controlled by altering the threshold TT.

To determine the appropriate threshold, we can first compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of SS under H0H_{0}, and then perform a binary search on the CDF table. The CDF of the above distribution can be computed using generating functions [40, 41, 42]. The generating function for a single uniform discrete variable over {1,2,⋯,m}\{1,2,\cdots,m\} is G⁡(x)=x+x2+⋯+xmmG(x)=\frac{x+x^{2}+\dots+x^{m}}{m}. For the sum of nn i.i.d discrete uniform random variables over {1,2,⋯,m}\{1,2,\cdots,m\}, the generating function is Gn​(x)=(x+x2+⋯+xmm)nG_{n}(x)=\left(\frac{x+x^{2}+\dots+x^{m}}{m}\right)^{n}.

To extract the probability density function (PDF), we expand the polynomial coefficients of Gn​(x)G_{n}(x) into a sequence. We then extract the coefficient of xtx^{t}, which gives Pr⁡(S=t)\Pr(S=t): Pr⁡(S=t)=[xt]​Gn​(x)\Pr(S=t)=[x^{t}]G_{n}(x). The polynomial coefficients of Gn​(x)G_{n}(x) can be efficiently computed using Fast Fourier transform (FFT) [43]. Then we can compute the CDF table leveraging the computed PDF, and use binary search on the CDF array to find the largest TT such that Pr⁡(S≤T)≤p\Pr(S\leq T)\leq p. The whole detection procedure of RepoMark is presented in Algorithm 2.

IV-D Improving the scalability of the code mark scheme

A remaining problem is that, for a lengthy code file, our current design cannot effectively utilize its information redundancies, as it only injects one mark for each file. To better utilize the information redundancy in lengthy code files, we further derive the case of renaming multiple different variables in a single file. We follow the notations used in Section IV-C. Under H0H_{0}, the core difference when injecting multiple marks is that, now xx is no longer a deterministic token sequence, but a random sequence, whose randomness is introduced by the random selection of previous renamed variables in the same file. Under H0H_{0}, ww is independent of xx. Denote the possible set of context string xx as 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We have:

Pr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w,x,t1),⋯,f⁡(w,x,tm)},f⁡(w,x,tr))=k)=1m​∑w′∈WPr⁡(w=w′)∑y=1mPr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w′,x,t1),⋯},f⁡(w′,x,ty))=k)=1m​∑w′∈WPr⁡(w=w′)​∑p∈𝒳Pr⁡(x=p)∑y=1mPr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w′,p,t1),⋯},f⁡(w′,p,ty))=k)\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w,x,t^{1}),\cdots,f(w,x,t^{m})\},f(w,x,t^{r}))=k)\\ =&\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w^{\prime}\in W}\Pr(w=w^{\prime})\\ &\sum_{y=1}^{m}\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w^{\prime},x,t^{1}),\cdots\},f(w^{\prime},x,t^{y}))=k)\\ =&\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w^{\prime}\in W}\Pr(w=w^{\prime})\sum_{p\in\mathcal{X}}\Pr(x=p)\\ &\sum_{y=1}^{m}\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w^{\prime},p,t^{1}),\cdots\},f(w^{\prime},p,t^{y}))=k)\end{aligned} (2)

Given pp, yy, w′w^{\prime}, each {f⁡(w′,p,t1),⋯}\{f(w^{\prime},p,t^{1}),\cdots\} is a deterministic set. Therefore,

∑y=1mPr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w′,p,t1),⋯},f⁡(w′,p,ty))=k)=1\sum_{y=1}^{m}\Pr\left(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w^{\prime},p,t^{1}),\cdots\},f(w^{\prime},p,t^{y}))=k\right)=1

Combining this with Equation 2, we have:

Pr⁡(𝗋𝗄⁡({f⁡(w,x,t1),⋯,f⁡(w,x,tm)},f⁡(w,x,tr))=k)=1m​∑w′∈WPr⁡(w=w′)​∑p∈𝒳Pr⁡(x=p)=1m\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\Pr(\mathsf{rk}(\{f(w,x,t^{1}),\cdots,f(w,x,t^{m})\},f(w,x,t^{r}))=k)\\ =&\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w^{\prime}\in W}\Pr(w=w^{\prime})\sum_{p\in\mathcal{X}}\Pr(x=p)\\ =&\frac{1}{m}\end{aligned}

The above equation shows that if the model weights ww are not trained on the file, then when multiple marks are injected into the same code file, the ranks of the published versions for each injected mark are still i.i.d variables, uniformly distributed over {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\}. This property ensures that RepoMark can support injecting multiple marks (i.e., renaming multiple variables) within a single file, making our method highly scalable to long code files.

We use mark sparsity threshold KK to control how many marks we should inject into one code file. Given mark sparsity threshold KK, at most one mark can be injected per KK lines of code. In other words, for a code file with LL lines of code, we only add at most ⌊LK⌋\lfloor\frac{L}{K}\rfloor marks. Following the previous construction, we only rename local variables whose first occurrence has an oracle model rank greater than or equal to the threshold RR. If there are more than ⌊LK⌋\lfloor\frac{L}{K}\rfloor candidate variables that satisfy this property, we randomly select ⌊LK⌋\lfloor\frac{L}{K}\rfloor variables among them. By choosing an appropriate KK value, we can effectively balance imperceptibility and detection accuracy. When a smaller KK is chosen, the detection would be more accurate as the injected mark number nn is larger. However, in the meantime, it would be easier for the model trainer to detect the mark.

IV-E Extending to the OpenAI API setting

We next describe how to adapt our algorithm to operate under a more restricted logits access setting, aligning with that of OpenAI API [38]. Specifically, OpenAI’s create completion API does not provide full access to the logits vector; instead, it only returns the log-probabilities of the top-20 tokens at each position via the 𝗍𝗈𝗉​_​𝗅𝗈𝗀𝗉𝗋𝗈𝖻𝗌\mathsf{top\_logprobs} parameter.

Our key adaptation leverages its 𝗅𝗈𝗀𝗂𝗍​_​𝖻𝗂𝖺𝗌\mathsf{logit\_bias} parameter, which enables adding specified biases to a set of selected tokens. By assigning a sufficiently large positive bias to a target token set, we can ensure these tokens to appear in the top 20, forcing the API to return their log-probabilities. Importantly, applying the same bias to all tokens preserves their relative logit rankings. This adaptation allows us to indirectly infer the relative ranking of any token set of up to 20 tokens at a given position. As a result, our detection algorithm remains compatible with the restricted logits access setting of the OpenAI API, provided the hyperparameter m≤20m\leq 20.

V Experiments

V-A Experimental setup

Models. We conduct experiments on data marking using CodeParrot-1.5B [14], StarCoder2-3B [46], and InCoder-6B [19] as target models. Among them, CodeParrot-1.5B is the earliest released code LLM, based on the architecture of GPT-2 [47]. StarCoder2-3B is a larger model in our experiment, with around 3 billion parameters. It employs advanced attention mechanisms and a significantly larger context window compared to the other models, potentially allowing for more complex code generation tasks. InCoder-6B, developed by Facebook, is a more advanced model boasting 6 billion parameters. It stands out for its ability to perform both standard left-to-right code generation and code infilling, making it a versatile tool for various coding tasks. For the oracle LLM leveraged by RepoMark, we use another code LLM Yi-Coder-1.5B [48].

Datasets. Our experiments are primarily carried out on three datasets, CodeParrot dataset [14], CodeSearchNet [49], and CodeNet [50]. Following prior work [51, 52, 53], we focus on Python code, though our techniques are also applicable to other languages such as C++, Java, and Rust. The CodeParrot dataset consists of Python code files sourced from GitHub public repositories, with duplicates removed and cleaning heuristics applied to ensure high-quality data. The dataset contains 5,170,318 rows of code, each with detailed features such as the repository name, GitHub path, license, etc., making it suitable for per-repository analysis. The CodeSearchNet dataset includes 2 million (comment, code) pairs written in Python and Java. The CodeNet dataset proposed by IBM research is also widely used. The dataset contains 4,053 problems and 7,460,588 accepted submissions across 55 languages.

To construct the training set for our experiments, we first choose the desired file count per repository NN and randomly select half of the repositories with file counts in the range [0.95​N,1.05​N][0.95N,1.05N] for mark injection. We further include unmarked repositories to simulate a realistic mixture of marked and unmarked data. Unlike prior works [5, 12] that focus on dataset-level auditing (i.e., producing a binary decision for the entire dataset), our detection algorithm performs binary classification at the repository level, determining whether each repository has been abused in training. This setting better reflects real-world auditing scenarios where the repository owner aims to identify which specific repositories have been used.

Metrics. We evaluate RepoMark along two dimensions: its detection accuracy, as well as its impact on code quality.

For detection accuracy, we measure it using the DSR metric, which captures the fraction of marked repositories in the training set that are successfully identified. Following Huang et al. [5], we measure the DSR under different FDR. For data mark methods that have theoretical FDR guarantee, we measure the DSR at different specified FDR gurantees; for methods that cannot provide a guarantee on FDR (e.g. membership inference methods), we measure the DSR at different specified empirical FDR. It is worth noting that although under experimental conditions, we can compute empirical FDR for no-FDR-guarantee methods using member and non-member labels of all samples, such labels are not available in real-world auditing. Therefore, the empirical FDR values for these methods are not computable outside of the experimental setting.

For code quality, we mainly measure the extent to which the data marking method alters the original code. We adopt three metrics: CodeBLEU, edit distance, and perplexity. CodeBLEU [54] is a classical metric to measure the quality of code adopted in previous works [55, 56, 57]. It extends the traditional BLEU metric by incorporating syntax and semantics specific to programming languages, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of the code generated. It measures the similarity between the original code and the marked code, using a weighted combination of n-gram match, weighted n-gram match, AST match, and data-flow match scores. Edit distance [58, 59] is a common metric used to measure the difference between two strings. It quantifies the minimum number of insertion, deletion, and substitution operations required to transform one string into another. In our paper, to quantify the quality of marked code, we measure the edit distance between marked code and original code on a per-token basis. We also adopt the perplexity (PPL) metric, which is widely adopted in the NLP community, following previous works [60, 61, 62, 63]. In our experiments, the PPL scores are computed using the Qwen2.5-Coder-7B [64] model.

Hyperparameters. In our experiments, we set the theoretical FDR guarantee to p=5%p=5\% and the number of mark versions to m=100m=100. The default repository file count is N=20N=20. We set the default repository file count to be small, as detecting training usage on a per-repository basis is significantly more challenging for smaller repositories than for larger ones. The mark sparsity parameter is set to K=100K=100 (i.e., on average, there is at most one mark per 100100 lines of code), and the mark position rank threshold is set to R=500R=500. For model training, the learning rate is initialized to 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, and the number of training epochs is limited to 2, in other words, the model sees each training code snippet twice.

AST Parser. We use the tree-sitter library [65, 66] to parse the code and perform transformations on AST. We first use tree-sitter to identify the function parameter names and variable names to inject our marks. After locating the marking positions, we utilize tree-sitter to perform variable renamings on the AST.

V-B Main results

RepoMark performs well on different models and datasets. We carry out the experiments with 3 different code models, CodeParrot-1.5B, StarCoder2-3B, and InCoder-6B, and 3 different datasets, CodeParrot, CodeSearchNet, and CodeNet. We measure the effectiveness of the data-usage detection of RepoMark method under different FDR guarantees 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, and the results are shown in Figure 4. We use default hyperparameter settings for these experiments. On the CodeParrot dataset, with FDR guarantee 5%, RepoMark achieves 90.08%, 98.64%, and 93.58% DSR on CodeParrot-1.5B, StarCoder2-3B, and InCoder-6B, respectively. These results show that we can detect more than 90% code training usage if these models are trained on our marked code. The performance of RepoMark is robust on three different datasets. Even under the worst case, it still achieves a DSR higher than 85%85\% under FDR guarantee 5%. These results demonstrate the strong generalizability of RepoMark under different models and datasets, indicating the potential value of deploying RepoMark as a tool in real-world data auditing.

RepoMark outperforms existing baselines. We also compare RepoMark with existing data usage auditing methods, which can be categorized into two types: (1) membership inference and (2) data marking. For membership inference-based methods, we compare against several prevalent approaches for LLMs, including loss-based membership inference [44], min-k inference [28], zlib-based membership inference [45], and dataset inference [32]. Except for dataset inference [31], all membership inference methods audit at the single-file level. For data marking-based methods, we compare against CodeMark [12] (FSE’23), the only existing data marking method designed for code models. Additionally, since the state-of-the-art data marking framework by Huang et al. [5] does not directly support the code domain, we adapt it to the code domain by replacing their marking phase with marking algorithm of RepoMark.

Since previous results demonstrate that our method performs consistently across different datasets and models, we conduct all baseline comparisons on the CodeParrot-1.5B model and the CodeParrot dataset due to resource constraints. The comparison results are shown in Table I. It is evident that RepoMark consistently outperforms all baselines under different configurations. Under 5% FDR guarantee, RepoMark achieves the highest DSR of 90.08%, significantly surpassing all membership inference-based methods and data marking methods. Under the same FDR, the best data marking method except ours can only achieve a DSR of 53.79%, while the best membership inference-based method only achieves a DSR of 18.68%. These methods fail to identify a large proportion of the trained repositories, whereas RepoMark only misidentifies 10% of the repositories used for training.

RepoMark achieves good imperceptibility. We measure RepoMark’s influence on code quality using CodeBLEU, edit distance, and PPL on CodeParrot dataset. According to Table II, RepoMark effectively preserves code quality with minimal changes, offering good marking imperceptibility. It achieves a high CodeBLEU score of 0.963. The change to the original code by RepoMark is minimal measured by edit distance. On average, only 3.61 tokens are modified per 100 lines of code. The PPL of our marked code is also very close to the PPL of unmarked code. This demonstrates that RepoMark’s modifications are unlikely to be noticed by human inspectors and remain mostly imperceptible to the model trainer.

RepoMark does not impact code LLM training. In addition, we observe that the impact of RepoMark to code LLM training is negligible. We employ the HumanEval dataset [67] to evaluate the performance of CodeParrot-1.5B trained with a (1) normal CodeParrot dataset and (2) CodeParrot dataset injected by RepoMark. Following HumanEval  [67], we measure the model performance with metric Pass@ kk [67], which measures the proportion of samples for which at least one of kk independently generated outputs passes the predefined unit tests. According to Table VII, training on dataset marked by RepoMark only has negligible influence on model performance measured by Pass@11, Pass@1010 and Pass@100100, respectively. Therefore, the model trainer is very unlikely to observe the existence of our mark via the code model’s capability.

V-C Ablation study

In this section, we discuss the key factors that influence the detection performance of RepoMark, including training parameters, dataset structure, and hyperparameters of our method.

Impact of mm. We first study the impact of the number of marking versions mm on DSR. As illustrated in Figure , DSR of our detection method improves as mm increases. Under the 5% FDR guarantee, the DSR increases steadily from 53.79% under m=2m=2 to 90.08% under m=100m=100. This is not surprising because when the number of versions mm increases, each position’s rank delivers more nuanced information, enabling more accurate detection. Another observation is that the effect of increasing mm on the detection accuracy is gradually diminishing: under the 5% FDR guarantee, the accuracy only increases by 5.64% (from 84.44% to 90.08%) when mm increases from 20 to 100. This indicates that when mm is sufficiently large, the information gain from generating more code variants (i.e., larger mm) is less significant.

Impact of NN. We also evaluate the impact of repository file count NN on the detection performance of RepoMark, and the results are shown in Figure . The detection accuracy increases with the growth of NN. When the repository file count increases to 40, DSR increases to over 90% even under 1% FDR guarantee. When the repository file count increases to N≥50N\geq 50, the DSR is 100% consistently with all FDR guarantee tested, which indicates that RepoMark successfully identify all repositories used in training under these settings. This trend aligns with our expectations because a larger repository file count enables more marking positions for detection, thus leading to a higher detection accuracy. These results highlight the effectiveness of RepoMark in auditing commercial-scale code repositories. At the same time, RepoMark also demonstrates strong capabilities in handling repositories with small sizes. Notably, RepoMark can achieve 73.79% DSR for an extremely small repository size (N=10N=10) under a 5% FDR guarantee, demonstrating its strong capability in protecting the copyright of individual users’ code.

Impact of KK. We further evaluate how the mark sparsity KK would influence the DSR of RepoMark, and the experiments results can be found in Figure . It can be observed that as KK increases, the DSR exhibits a gradual decline while RepoMark still remains usable. When K=50K=50, our detection method achieves 100% detection accuracy under all FDR guarantees. With KK increasing to 200, the DSR under 5% FDR guarantee is still higher than 70%, indicating that our detection method demonstrates high robustness regardless of KK. It is worth noting that while using a smaller KK can improve detection performance, it also leads to the deterioration in code quality. As shown in Table III, KK affects edit distance in a nearly proportional way. When K≥100K\geq 100, both PPL and CodeBLEU remain quite close to the unmarked case, indicating that code quality is not significantly impacted. In contrast, when KK is reduced to 50, the CodeBLEU drops to 0.8059, which indicates a noticeable degradation in code quality. In conclusion, K=100K=100 is a proper choice to balance the trade-off between code quality and detection performance.

Impact of Logits Access Restriction. We further compare the performance of our model under two different threat model settings: full logits access (our default) and the restricted logits access setting imposed by the OpenAI API [38]. Since the ground-truth training data of OpenAI’s GPT-4 is unavailable, we simulate the API’s behavior using our local LLMs. The results are shown in Figure 7 in the Appendix. Remarkably, even under the restricted setting, our method achieves a DSR above 80% while ensuring a 5% FDR guarantee, highlighting its practicality under more constrained and realistic conditions.

V-D Deployment overhead

In this section, we discuss and explore the deployment overhead of our algorithm.

Marking overhead. Our marking algorithm is highly efficient because the main computational overhead of marking each file lies in a single forward pass of each file through the oracle code LLM, during which full vocabulary logits are computed for all positions. We measured that marking one repository with 20 files takes 15.6 seconds on average.

Storage overhead. The storage overhead of our algorithm is also minimal. For detection purposes, we only need to store the original token (prior to marking) and its position within the file. This information is sufficient to reconstruct the list of alternative tokens at each marked position. Under our default setting of K=100K=100—i.e., at most one mark per 100 lines of code—the average number of marked positions per file is about 3. Each marked position requires 4 bytes of storage: 2 bytes for the token ID and 2 bytes for its position. Therefore, for a large repository with 100 files, the total storage overhead is approximately 1.2KB, which is negligible.

Detection overhead. Our detection process mainly requires computing the relative logit ranks of the mm token variants at each marked position, which can be obtained in a single forward pass of the code file through the LLM. Since detection typically relies on model APIs that charge per token, we estimate the cost in terms of the total number of LLM tokens processed. Under our default logits access setting, the user cost for detecting a repository is proportional to the total number of tokens across all NN files of the repository. For example, a large commercial repository such as the React library [68] contains around 4 million tokens. Given that current LLM APIs charge less than 10−610^{-6} USD per token, the detection cost for a repository of this scale is only a few dollars.

Under the restricted logits access setting, the detection cost increases primarily because the OpenAI API does not support changing the set of biased tokens across different positions. As a result, we must perform a separate forward pass for each marked position. For a given code file with SS marked positions, this amounts to SS forward passes. The average SS per-file is about 3. Thus, detecting whether GPT-4 was trained on a large commercial repository like React is estimated to cost less than $20, which remains negligible compared to the repository’s development cost.

Version control strategy. Since code files in real-world repositories are frequently updated, a version control strategy can be adopted to avoid reinjecting marks after every change. As long as the marked tokens remain unmodified, we simply update the stored marking positions to reflect the changes. New mark injection is only required when previously marked tokens are deleted, or when the user adds a substantial amount of new code that creates additional capacity for marking. In real-world auditing, to reduce detection overhead, we can choose to run the detection algorithm only on each “major version” of the repository—i.e., versions that differ substantially from the previous ones. Our detection algorithm’s FDR guarantee still holds for each individual detection, although the results across different detections may be statistically dependent.

V-E Potential countermeasures of the model trainer

In this section, we explore several potential countermeasures against our marking algorithm.

Early stopping [69, 70, 71] is a widely deployed strategy to reduce the model’s memorization to training data. We show the impact of different training epochs to DSR in Figure 6. It can be observed that, the performance of RepoMark drops with the decrease of training epochs. When the model is trained for 33 epoches, RepoMark can identify almost all trained repositories under the FDR guarantee of 5%. However, when the number of epochs decreases to 11, the DSR reduces to 60.31%. This aligns with the classical observations between training epochs and memorization in  [72, 73, 74, 75]. Additionally, from Table VI in Appendix, it can be observed that the training process requires at least 2-3 epochs to converge. This indicates that early stopping is not effective in preventing RepoMark’s detection. If the model trainer tends to train an effective model using unauthorized code, he has to face the trade-off between model quality and the risk of being caught by RepoMark.

Dataset filtering [76, 77, 78, 79] is a class of techniques that were initially proposed to identify and remove backdoored data from the training corpus. Following CodeMark [12], we evaluate two typical dataset filtering strategies, activation clustering [76] and spectral signature [77]. The model trainer will use the aforementioned methods to remove the code files that are identified as marked from the training dataset. To evaluate the effectiveness of dataset filtering method, we compute both the proportion of unmarked code removed from the unmarked dataset and the proportion of marked code removed from the marked dataset. The results are shown in Table V in Appendix. It can be observed that both activation clustering and spectral signature are ineffective in removing our mark. For both methods, their removal ratio on marked code is similar to unmarked code, indicating that they essentially performs random guessing on which code files to remove code within the dataset. Moreover, at a 5% FDR, RepoMark still achieves 78.4% and 86.6% DSR under the two removal strategies respectively. These results validate RepoMark’s resilience against auto-removal of the model trainer.

We also evaluate variable renaming as an adaptive attack strategy against RepoMark, where the model trainer (attacker) randomly renames a certain proportion of variables to neutralize the embedded marks. The core idea is to aggressively rename variables in the training data to “cover” those renamed by RepoMark. To enhance the attack, the adaptive trainer can leverage an oracle code LLM to select variables for renaming that fall within the same logits rank range targeted by our marking algorithm. Importantly, we assume the attacker does not know which oracle model each user employs, as the training dataset consists of code written by a large number of users, each potentially using a different oracle code LLM.

We evaluate this strategy under renaming ratios of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%, with detection results presented in Table IV. When the renaming ratio is at or below 75%, the impact on RepoMark’s detection performance remains minimal—across different oracle code LLMs, our system continues to achieve DSR >75%>75\% under 5% FDR guarantee. Even when the attacker renames all tokens proposed by the oracle code LLM (i.e., 100% renaming), RepoMark still successfully identifies over 65% of the training repositories. This robustness stems from the variation in logits rankings across different oracle models, making it difficult for an attacker using oracle A to accurately obscure the marks generated by oracle B.

Notably, such aggressive renaming alters code context and harms code quality and readability. To evaluate the utility loss, we trained the CodeParrot-1.5B model with an 100% renaming ratio. The model’s Pass@100 score dropped from 15.24% (no renaming) to 12.78%, indicating that excessive variable renaming impairs model training. This poses a significant challenge for attackers: without knowledge of the exact oracle used, it is difficult to suppress RepoMark effectively and maintain model performance simultaneously.

VI Conclusion

The widespread deployment of code LLMs has raised pressing ethical and legal concerns about the unauthorized use of code repositories. In this paper, we propose a proactive data auditing framework tailored to the code domain, which achieves both high detection accuracy and provable FDR guarantees. Through extensive experiments, we show that our framework significantly outperforms existing auditing methods in detection accuracy. These results highlight the potential of our approach to empower repository owners to verify whether their code has been used in training code LLMs.
